examples.name: Overview
examples.code:
const [returnsDisabled, setReturnsDisabled] = useState(false)

<Accordion type="single" collapsible defaultValue="shipping">
  <Accordion.Item value="shipping">
    <Accordion.Trigger>What are your shipping options?</Accordion.Trigger>
    <Accordion.Content>
      We offer standard (5–7 business days), express (2–3 days), and overnight shipping…
    </Accordion.Content>
  </Accordion.Item>
  <Accordion.Item value="returns" disabled={returnsDisabled}>
    <Accordion.Trigger>What is your return policy?</Accordion.Trigger>
    <Accordion.Content>Returns are accepted within 30 days of delivery…</Accordion.Content>
  </Accordion.Item>
  <Accordion.Item value="support">
    <Accordion.Trigger>How can I contact customer support?</Accordion.Trigger>
    <Accordion.Content>Reach us by email, live chat, or phone Monday–Friday…</Accordion.Content>
  </Accordion.Item>
</Accordion>
examples.details: Set type to multiple when readers can keep several sections open at once: settings pages, long FAQs, step-by-step references. A single accordion with collapsible lets readers close the open item; without it one item is always open. card composes the accordion inside Card, the most common landing-page FAQ pattern; on a phone the card is a section of the grouped list. The returnsDisabled control disables only the return-policy item. It remains visible and keeps its open state, while keyboard navigation skips its trigger.

components.name: Alert
components.description: Inline message for notices and warnings with semantic colors, variants, a title, a description, action slots, and a dismiss control.

props.name: title
props.description: Title displayed in the alert

props.name: description
props.description: Description text

props.name: actions
props.description: Actions (for example buttons)

props.name: actionsPlacement
props.description: Placement of actions; automatic from sizing when unset

props.name: mobileActions
props.description: At 767px and below: 50px capsules as in an iOS tip, or the buttons at their own size, for an alert inside a block of its own buttons

props.name: actionsClassName
props.description: Class applied to the actions container

props.name: color
props.description: Color scheme

props.name: variant
props.description: Style variant

props.name: indicator
props.description: Custom indicator or false to hide

props.name: onDismiss
props.description: Shows the dismiss button when set

props.name: banner
props.description: Full-width strip: square corners, lines above and below only

props.name: className
props.description: Class applied to the alert container

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: color and variant style the alert. It shows a title, a description or both; each takes text or nodes, such as a <TextLink color="currentcolor"> to a status page. It has an indicator icon by default, chosen from its color: an icon in indicator replaces it, and indicator={'{false}'} hides it. actions takes buttons or other nodes. They are placed automatically, at the end or, when they take more than a third of the alert's width, under the message, unless actionsPlacement is 'end' or 'bottom'. onDismiss adds a Dismiss button in the alert's chrome; for a dismissible notice, labeled buttons in actions are the suggested approach. A solid alert is for a message alone: buttons, Dismiss among them, do not read on its color, so this preview offers them on soft and outline alerts. Use banner for a full-width strip across the top or bottom of a page or panel (offline, read-only, a new version): it drops the rounded corners and keeps only the lines above and below. On a phone an alert takes the shape and text of an iOS tip (TipKit), the system's message inside a screen: 26px corners (a banner stays square), the title at 17/22 semibold and the description at 15/20, and a close button in its corner instead of Dismiss. A title or a description alone stands its first line on the middle of the icon. It keeps its icon, colors and variants, and its actions always stand under the message as 50px capsules side by side, so actionsPlacement is a desktop setting. With mobileActions="own" the actions keep the size you give the buttons, for an alert inside a block of its own buttons.

components.name: Avatar
components.description: An avatar for user identities that shows an initial, a photo or an icon, with overflow counts, semantic colors and roundness options.

props.name: name
props.description: Display name; used for text initial when no image/icon

props.name: imageUrl
props.description: Absolute URL for image avatar

props.name: Icon
props.description: Icon component for icon avatar

props.name: size
props.description: Width and height in pixels

props.name: color
props.description: Semantic color for text/icon avatar

props.name: variant
props.description: Style variant

props.name: overflowCount
props.description: Show overflow count (e.g. +9)

props.name: className
props.description: Applied to the avatar root

props.name: onClick
props.description: Makes avatar interactive (renders a button)

props.name: onPointerDown
props.description: Makes avatar interactive (renders a button)

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: An avatar shows one of four things. Without other props it shows the first letter of name. With imageUrl, an absolute URL, it shows the photo with a soft fade once it loads, and the initial if it fails. With Icon, an icon component such as Robot from @plexui/ui/components/Icon, it shows the icon; name is not shown, and only names the avatar when it is a button. With overflowCount it shows the count, formatted and scaled to fit. size sets the width and height in pixels, and the initial, icon and count scale with it. color and variant style every avatar except a loaded photo, which covers them. Avatars are fully rounded by default; a Tailwind rounding class in className overrides that. An onClick (or onPointerDown) handler makes the avatar a button with interaction styles and its name as the accessible name.

props.name: separator

props.name: aria-label

props.name: className

examples.name: Overview
examples.code:
<Breadcrumb>
<Breadcrumb.Item href="/">Home</Breadcrumb.Item>

An item with href is a link (internal paths use the linkComponent of PlexUIProvider, such as your router's link); the current item is plain text marked aria-current="page". iOS has no breadcrumb, a phone screen goes back with the back button of its Toolbar. A trail kept on a phone takes the 15/20 text of iOS and gives each link a 44px touch target.

components.name: Button Group
components.description: Join buttons into a single visual unit for toolbars, steppers, split buttons and search affordances.

props.name: orientation
props.description: Direction of the joined items

props.name: mobileMaterial
props.description: Phone surface with touch.css: "glass" makes the group one glass capsule outside a Toolbar, "flat" keeps the joined buttons in one

props.name: className
props.description: Applied to the root <div>

examples.name: Overview
examples.code:
const [size, setSize] = useState("sm")

// Desktop
<ButtonGroup>
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="Go back">
    <ArrowLeftSm />
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size}>Pin</Button>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size}>Tag</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size}>Bookmark</Button>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="More options">
    <DotsHorizontal />
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
</ButtonGroup>

// Phone: the bars of a note
<Page>
<Toolbar>
  <Toolbar.Leading>
    <NavigationButton action="back" />
  </Toolbar.Leading>
  <Toolbar.Trailing>
    <ButtonGroup aria-label="Note actions">
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Pin"><Pin /></Button>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Tag"><Tag /></Button>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="More"><DotsHorizontal /></Button>
    </ButtonGroup>
  </Toolbar.Trailing>
</Toolbar>
<Page.Content>…</Page.Content>
<Toolbar placement="bottom">
  <Toolbar.Leading>
    <ButtonGroup aria-label="Editing tools">
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Checklist"><NotebookCheck /></Button>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Attach"><Clip /></Button>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Markup"><Pens /></Button>
    </ButtonGroup>
  </Toolbar.Leading>
  <Toolbar.Trailing>
    <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="New note"><PencilSquare /></Button>
  </Toolbar.Trailing>
</Toolbar>
</Page>
examples.details: Set size on every Button inside the group so corner radii match; the size setting here sets all of them. Mix icon-only (uniform) with text buttons; each child keeps its own padding. On a phone with touch.css a group in the content keeps one height. Beside text buttons its icon-only buttons take the heights of the iOS small (28px, sm) and medium (34px, md and lg) buttons; a group of icon-only buttons keeps their 44px, and beside a text field or a select every button takes the field's 44px. Joined segments have no iOS control of their own. On a phone the example is the bars of a note, as in iOS Notes: Back alone, the note's actions in one glass capsule on top, the editing tools in one at the bottom beside New Note. A ButtonGroup in a Toolbar is that capsule, as iOS 27.2 sets it: 44px buttons 10px apart in a 154px capsule on top, 48px ones 8px apart in a 164px capsule at the bottom, the symbols in the primary label color. Groups side by side stand apart as the bar's items do. The bar sets its buttons' size, so the phone view leaves out the size control.

examples.name: Orientation
examples.code:
const [size, setSize] = useState("sm")

// Desktop
<ButtonGroup orientation="vertical" aria-label="Zoom controls">
<Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="Zoom in">
  <PlusSm />
</Button>
<Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="Zoom out">
  <Minus />
</Button>
</ButtonGroup>

// Phone: zoom controls over a canvas
<ButtonGroup orientation="vertical" mobileMaterial="glass" aria-label="Zoom controls" className="absolute top-2 right-4">
<Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Zoom in"><Plus /></Button>
<Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Zoom out"><Minus /></Button>
</ButtonGroup>
examples.details: Pass orientation="vertical" to stack the buttons, useful for + / − steppers, zoom controls, or any vertical toolbar. On a phone the example is zoom controls floating over a canvas, as map controls do: with mobileMaterial="glass" the group is the vertical Button Group of the iOS 27 kit, a 48px wide capsule of 48px buttons 6px apart. In the content a group of icon-only buttons keeps their 44px at each size, so the phone view leaves out the size control.

examples.name: Input group
examples.details: Richer composition for message composers: wrap each slot (leading action, flexible Input) in its own ButtonGroup so the outer group inserts a gap between them. The voice toggle rides inside the input via endAdornment. Use Input.AdornmentButton: it sizes off the input's own size token so the button stays concentric with the pill at every size. On a phone with touch.css the buttons take the field's 44px at each size shown, so the phone view leaves out the size control.

examples.name: Nested
examples.code:
const [size, setSize] = useState("sm")

<ButtonGroup aria-label="Pager">
<ButtonGroup>
  {[1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((page) => (
    <Button key={page} variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size}>{page}</Button>
  ))}
</ButtonGroup>
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="Previous page">
    <ArrowLeftSm />
  </Button>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="Next page">
    <ArrowRightSm />
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
</ButtonGroup>
examples.details: Place ButtonGroup inside ButtonGroup to create visually separated sub-groups. The outer group automatically adds a small gap between children; pagination with arrow navigation is the canonical pattern.

examples.name: Separator
examples.code:
const [size, setSize] = useState("sm")

<ButtonGroup>
<Button variant="soft" color="secondary" size={size}><Undo /> Undo</Button>
<ButtonGroup.Separator />
<Button variant="soft" color="secondary" size={size}>Redo <Redo /></Button>
</ButtonGroup>
examples.details: Drop a ButtonGroup.Separator between items to add a visible divider, commonly used for Undo / Redo pairs or any "two related actions" toolbar. A glass group on a phone draws no line, as the capsule of iOS has none.

examples.name: Split
examples.code:
const [size, setSize] = useState("sm")

<ButtonGroup>
<Button variant="soft" color="secondary" size={size}><Filter /> Filter</Button>
<ButtonGroup.Separator />
<Button variant="soft" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="Add filter">
  <Plus />
</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
examples.details: The classic split button: an action joined to a secondary affordance via ButtonGroup.Separator. Useful for Save / Save-As, Filter / Add-filter, Delete / Undo.

examples.name: Input
examples.code:
const [size, setSize] = useState("sm")

<ButtonGroup>
<Input placeholder="Search docs..." size={size} />
<Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} aria-label="Search">

</Button>
</ButtonGroup>

examples.name: Select

On a phone with touch.css the button takes the height of the 44px fields at each size shown, so the phone view leaves out the size control.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: On a phone a dialog is one of the two modal views of iOS: an Alert (mobileVariant="alert"), a short question with its answers, or a Sheet, which it is by default (see Placement). The alert takes what the iOS 27 kit and UIAlertController offer. One, two or three actions: two stand side by side with Cancel first, and three or more stack in their order with Cancel last, as iOS sets them. Dialog.Footer mobileLayout="stacked" stacks two, for long labels. The main action is preferred (solid: the accent fill on a phone), plain (soft), or destructive (color="danger": a red label on the alert's fill on a phone). A title without a message stands centered. A field asks for one short value: a 48px capsule on a phone, its text selected when the alert opens, and Rename unavailable while it is empty. Label actions in title case, as iOS does.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: An empty message is made of parts, each optional: an icon, a title, a description and an action row. It needs a title or a description, so this preview offers description with a title; the description takes text or nodes, such as a search term in font-semibold. color on EmptyMessage.Icon and on EmptyMessage.Title shows the intent of the message, such as danger on both for an error (a missing permission) or warning on the icon for a notice (a feature in beta); the description keeps its own color. fill sizes the message to its parent: static takes the full width and height, absolute covers a positioned parent, and none applies no sizing, for a container that sets the height (a list with no results). Use size="sm" for an empty panel, card section or list: a smaller title, tighter spacing, no minimum width and a small icon badge; in a message of the default size the icon takes its own size. align="start" left-aligns the message, for an empty state under a section heading: a single line such as "No tags added" reads with the heading above it. The action row takes buttons, or a TextLink with className="text-sm" on the row. On a phone a message of the default size takes the shape of the kit's empty state: the symbol in a 64px slot, a 22px bold title over a 17px description, and its buttons 24px under the text, one at its own width and two across the width one under the other. A message that fills a screen puts its buttons across the screen at its bottom, as iOS does, the main one on top, and centres the text in the space above them; a second action reads best as a plain button.

The layout control puts the label in its four places: above: the default, orientation="vertical". columns: orientation="horizontal", every value starting at one column. end: row, one line of a FieldGroup with the value at its end. A framed field is a pill there and takes --field-row-control-width, as its width cannot follow what is typed; pill={'{false}'} on the control keeps the rounded box. hidden: hideLabel. The label still names the control for screen readers; the placeholder shows what to type, and a description moves under the field. On Phone a field is always a cell of a FieldGroup on the grouped background, as in an iOS form, in the same four places: the label above its value (row orientation="vertical"), values in one column (FieldGroup columns), the value at the end of the row, or the placeholder alone (row hideLabel), its value starting at the row's edge. The row is the field's frame, so a framed or soft field loses its frame. The error stands inside the cell, under the value. The words that explain a field go in the group's footer, and a required field says so in its placeholder, as iOS account forms do. A disabled field dims its label with its value. A one-time code is the exception: OTPInput keeps its own digit cells on the screen, outside a group, as in Verify email.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: Two things set the type: where the label rests (labelPlacement: on the border, or inside the box with the value under it), and the shape of the field. Text fields, textareas and selects take both settings the same way. Both floating fields follow the same two tokens, so a form can set its radius and gutter in one place. Choose Empty or Filled to replace the value with a preset. The other controls preserve your text. Invalid and errorMessage demonstrate visual states, not email validation. An error message also marks the field invalid, so invalid is offered only without one; when both messages are enabled, the error appears before the description. Read-only text can still be selected and copied. onClear shows a built-in clear button: it appears when the field has a value and is not disabled or read-only, and focus returns to the field. On Phone the field is a cell named by its placeholder: the label does not float and the cell is the frame, so labelPlacement and pill are desktop settings. examples.name: Overview
examples.details: indicator picks one of the three. LoadingIndicator is a spinner for general loading states. It takes the surrounding font-size and text color by default; size and strokeWidth set its size and stroke in pixels, a text class such as text-danger (or --indicator-color) colors it, and --indicator-rotate-duration sets the time of one turn. On a desktop it is a turning ring. With the optional touch stylesheet it is the iOS 27 spinner of eight rounded spokes: 20px by default, also inside a field (an Input adornment, an InputGroup addon or a SelectControl, through --control-indicator-size); up to 16px it takes the Small spokes and from 28px the Large ones. A strokeWidth replaces the spokes' widths, so the Phone view leaves it unset. CircularProgress is a progress ring. Without progress it simulates progress over maxDuration milliseconds, and done fills the ring and ends the simulation; this preview sets it every 4 seconds to start over. progress, from 0 to 100, shows a fixed value instead. size and strokeWidth (at most 4) size the ring, and trackColor and trackActiveColor color its track and its progress. LoadingDots shows typing progress with staggered pulsing dots in the current text color.

examples.details: Use variant to stylize the input. ghost has no border and no fill, for a field its container already frames, such as the search line at the top of a dialog; it still turns red when invalid. The state control shows each variant empty, with a value, invalid and disabled. examples.name: Overview
examples.details: The header has no line at rest. Scroll the content: the line comes after 4px and goes again at the top. Turn divider off to keep the header without it. A page with fill does not scroll under its header, so on desktop the line does not come and the divider is offered without fill; on a phone only a glass or hard header draws the line, so there the divider is offered with those. width belongs to the page, so the line, the title, the buttons and the content always stand in one column. Take full for tables, wide for overviews and column for settings and forms; for any other width set --page-width on the page. This frame is narrower than a screen, so the preview shows both widths at half their size. fill stops the page scrolling from 768px up, so a table can scroll inside itself. On a phone a page takes the width of the screen at every width and scrolls as a whole, so the phone has neither setting. Page.Heading groups the title with metadata in Page.Subtitle. On a phone the badge and subtitle share a second row below the centered title. The header grows when metadata wraps, and the content keeps the corresponding space below it. Page.Leading holds a Back button or the menu button of a sidebar, before the title; on a phone the title stays centred between it and the actions. On a phone background sets how the header and the footer meet the content scrolled under them, as a Toolbar does: glass, the header's default, is a translucent, blurred bar with a hairline, soft, the footer's default, blurs the content under a header behind a thin veil of the canvas color and under the footer's actions the bottom edge of iOS 27.2, a blur behind a veil that grows toward the screen's edge, once content runs on under them, hard is an opaque bar with a hairline, and blur blurs the content under the bar, the more toward the screen's edge, with no fill and no line. Glass, hard and blur show themselves once content is under the bar. surface="grouped" gives the phone canvas the gray of grouped rows; desktop colors stay. The footer and its background stand under the preview, as what sits at the bottom of the screen.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: SegmentedControl provides two visual variants: segmented (default) with a sliding background highlight, and underline with an animated line indicator under the active tab and no background container. flush makes the underline indicator match the text width exactly, with gap between tabs instead of padding, and block stretches the tabs evenly across the container. orientation="vertical" stacks the tabs: the thumb slides up and down, and the underline becomes a line on the left side, for sidebar-style navigation. Both variants take the full 9-step size scale of Button, Input, Select and SelectControl, which sets the height, font size, icon size and spacing of the tabs. icon on a tab puts an icon before its label, sized to the size; leave out the label for icon-only tabs of a horizontal control and give each an aria-label. Vertical tabs keep their labels, so the example offers no icon only there: they are a list, a sidebar or on a phone an inset grouped list, and a list row always has a title. badge takes a number or an object with content, color, variant and pill, shown after the label inside the control; a count names what it counts, so it sits on a labelled tab and icon-only tabs carry none. disabled affects the whole group, which on a phone shows at half opacity when horizontal, as a disabled iOS segmented control does; monthDisabled disables only Month, whose label in a horizontal control on a phone takes the disabled label of iOS, 20% of the label color, while its row in a vertical one shows at half opacity. Arrow-key navigation skips disabled tabs without resetting the selected value.On a phone horizontal tabs of either variant are the iOS 27 segmented control, filling the row of a phone screen, in its two sizes. The default md and larger are the large control of iOS 27 apps, as Calendar and Reminders draw it and SwiftUI draws a segmented Picker in a toolbar: a 48px glass capsule, a 40px gray selection 4px inside it, 8px between segments, every label 15px Medium and primary. sm and smaller are the small one, the plain control of SwiftUI's Picker in content and of Safari's bookmarks: a 32px capsule of the tertiary fill, a white selection 2px inside it, labels 13px, Semibold when selected. mobileMaterial switches the look, as for Button: flat makes the large one plain, 49px as SwiftUI's .controlSize(.large), and glass puts the small one under the Liquid Glass of .glassEffect(). Inside a phone Toolbar every control is the large glass one. The phone example puts the control in a top bar between Close and Confirm, as a sheet's toolbar holds a segmented Picker in iOS 27.2 and Calendar its new event, in a bottom bar, or above the content, as Safari's bookmarks do, over a day that scrolls under the glass of the bars; placement picks one. Vertical tabs of either variant are an inset grouped list, as iOS lists a choice: 52px rows with the 17px label and a checkmark on the selected row instead of the thumb. A segment with an icon and a label shows the icon alone, at the 20px symbol size, as UISegmentedControl draws an action with a title and an image; the label stays the segment's accessible name, since iOS segments carry a title or a symbol, not both. They carry no badges either: on a phone write a count into the label instead, or leave it out. Underline tabs draw the same segmented control on a phone and every control there is a capsule filling its row, so the phone view has no variant, flush, block, pill and badge controls, and its size offers sm and md.

examples.details: Use variant to stylize the control: its styles are like those of {""}, with the small differences of {""}, and ghost has no frame. size sets the control's height, font size, gutter and the placement of its icon and indicator, on the 9-step scale of Button, Input, Select and SegmentedControl; pill rounds it fully and widens its gutter, and its clear action is a pill too. StartIcon puts an icon before the value, sized, spaced and colored by the control, and dropdownIconType picks the indicator. selected says the control holds a value and turns off the placeholder styling. It does nothing to the content, which is up to you, so here it follows the value: pick a period, or clear it. Pass onClearClick to make the control clearable: the clear action shows while it is selected. During loading the dropdown icon and clear action are hidden, the control is marked aria-busy and it ignores pointer and keyboard interaction; add disabled to dim it as well. invalid marks the control invalid; pair it with the field's errorMessage. disabled disables it both visually and accessibly. block stretches it across its container, here the 290px field. opticallyAlign offsets the control by its gutter: "start" puts the start of a ghost control, its icon or its text, on the label's edge, and "end" puts the end of a block one, its indicator, on the field's end. components.description: Toast notifications for transient feedback, with semantic variants, descriptions, action buttons, promise integration, and persistent toasts.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: Call toast with a message, or toast.success, .error, .warning and .info for the semantic types, which map to PlexUI's success, danger, warning and info tokens. Each of them shows its icon; icon: null leaves it out, and icon takes an element of your own instead. No richColors is passed, so the types retheme with data-theme. The options add a description under the message, an action button and a cancel one (either closes the toast after its onClick), and closeButton. toast.promise ties one toast to an async operation: it shows a loading state, then swaps to success or error, and takes the same options; here saveProfile() resolves with {"{ name: \"Profile\" }"} after 1.5 seconds. Spread compact into the options for a centered toast: on a desktop a toast shrinks to its content anyway, and on a phone, where a toast fills the width, a compact one keeps the width of its content. duration: Infinity keeps a toast open until the user closes it, so give it a labelled action or a close button: a way to close it from the keyboard. An error that waits like this is an alert (see Screen readers). On a desktop the message and its controls share a row: the buttons stand 16px after the message and 8px apart, small 28px buttons with 6px corners (the action solid, the cancel soft), and the close button is the same 28px button, plain, at the end. With a description the buttons go under the message, at the end, and the close button stays on the title's line. On a phone a toast takes the corners, padding and text of an iOS notification banner, the system's own message at the top of the screen: 24px corners and 15pt text, with its buttons drawn as a medium phone Button, a 34px capsule in a 44px target. One button stands at the end of the message's row, where a banner shows its time, and the message wraps in its own column; a cancel and an action together stand under the message, and so does a button that would leave the message less than half the row (8em in a toast as wide as its content). Under 600px it fills the width between 14px gutters past the safe area, as notifications do on an iOS phone; a compact toast keeps its own width. It stays a message of the page, with an opaque surface.

components.name: Toolbar
components.description: "The top and bottom bars of a phone screen: navigation, a title, a search field and actions over the content. Desktop layouts have their own composition, so a toolbar never renders from 768px up."

props.name: placement
props.description: Top bar with 44px targets, or bottom bar with 48px targets

props.name: titleStyle
props.description: Size and place of Toolbar.Title in a top bar

props.name: titleAlign
props.description: Alignment of an inline title. Large and compact titles always start at the leading edge

props.name: background
props.default: "glass" at the top, "soft" at the bottom
props.description: How the bar meets the content scrolled under it, see Background. "edge" is the earlier name of "soft" and "solid" of "hard"

props.name: className
props.description: Applied to the bar

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: Leading and trailing items take 44px targets; an inline title is centered across the whole width. titleStyle sets the size and place of the title: inline in the row of controls, large on a row of its own below them (on a page it stands at the top of the content and scrolls with it, overscroll included; once it has gone under the controls, they show it inline), and compact-large or compact-medium at the leading edge of the row, on a screen with no Back button. subtitle adds a second line under an inline or large title. titleAlign="start" puts an inline title after the leading items. Scroll the content: the bar's background meets the rows under it, and the glass starts to cast a shadow. Toolbar.Group puts related actions in one capsule; a single action, as Back or Close, keeps a capsule of its own. Without Toolbar.Title the bar holds its controls alone. A ButtonGroup in a toolbar is the same capsule. Name each icon button with aria-label. Toolbar.Content fill stretches a search field across the row in the place of the title, up to the trailing items; the field takes the row height and the material of the bar buttons. That is the open search: until a tap opens it, the search waits in a field across a row under the controls (search row) or behind a Search button in the bar (search button), and Close puts it back, as iOS 27.2 raises the field of the bar's drawer into the bar and hides the title and the buttons; a segmented row stays under the open field. Toolbar.Row adds a row under the controls, part of the bar: a SegmentedControl that switches the screen's views, as a chat list shows its folders under its bar, or a search field. It spans the bar between its gutters, 10px under the controls, and the bar's background and line take it in. Several rows stand in their order, 10px apart: a search field over a segmented control, as iOS 27.2 sets them under the search field of a bar's drawer. A segmented control in it is the small plain one at its default size (32px, as iOS 27.2 draws a segmented Picker under a bar) and fills the row: its segments share the width and scroll when they do not fit, and a badge counts what a view holds; size="lg" gives the large glass one (48px). A search field in it is the bar's: 44px of glass. Under a large title on a page the rows stand under the title at the top of the content, 16px under its baseline; scrolled up to the bar they stay pinned under its controls, and the bar's background, edge and line reach under them, as iOS 27.2 pins them. placement="bottom" sets the bar at the bottom of the page with 48px targets and the device's bottom safe area. Toolbar.Content centers a main action; with fill a search field or a single action takes the whole row. The 48px items stand 28px from the sides and above the home indicator, 12px apart, whatever the background: iOS 27.2 keeps them in place over every scroll edge, and a band (glass or hard) only starts 10px above them. A search field holds SearchSm, set in Regular; a plus next to it takes iconSize="sm", as Contacts draws it smaller than the other symbols. The page content scrolls under both bars. A screen holds one search field, so with one in the top bar the bottom bar offers neither its own field nor its Search button. background sets how a bar meets the content scrolled under it. glass, the default of a top bar, is a translucent, blurred bar with a hairline. soft, the default of a bottom bar, is the scroll edge effect of iOS 26 and draws no line: once content is under a top bar with a title, a blur hides it under the controls and lets go of it past the bar, under a thin veil of the canvas color (iOS 27.2: 55% at the top, 20% at the bar's bottom, none 24px below), while a top bar of controls alone on a page covers only the status bar, and once content runs on under a bottom bar on a page, a blur hides it under the controls behind a veil of the canvas color that grows toward the screen's edge, with no band and no line (iOS 27.2: none 34px above the items, 15% at their top, 46% from 43px into them); each glass control stands out over it. A Sheet's bottom bar fades its content into the panel. hard is an opaque bar of the canvas color with a hairline. blur has no fill and no line: the content under the bar is blurred a little over the bar and past it, and heavily toward the screen's edge. Glass, hard and blur show themselves once content is under the bar: under the top bar after the content has scrolled, over the bottom bar while it continues below. Page.Header, Page.Footer, the bars of a Sheet and TabBar take the same values. The top and the bottom bar each take their own; the bottom bar's controls stand under the preview.

examples.name: Search in the content
examples.code:
<Page surface="grouped">
<Toolbar titleStyle="large">
  <Toolbar.Title>Orders</Toolbar.Title>
  <Toolbar.Trailing>
    <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="More"><DotsHorizontal /></Button>
  </Toolbar.Trailing>
</Toolbar>
<Page.Content>
  <Input
    type="search"
    variant="soft"
    pill
    placeholder="Search"
    aria-label="Search orders"
    startAdornment={<SearchSm />}
    value={query}
    onChange={(evt) => setQuery(evt.target.value)}
    onClear={() => setQuery("")}
    className="mb-2.5"
  />
  ...
</Page.Content>
</Page>
examples.details: A search field in the content, under a large title or at the top of a sheet, is an Input with type="search": on Phone its magnifier stands where it does in the bar's field and its text 1px nearer, and variant="soft" pill gives it the flat fill of iOS 27, as in Files and a search tab. It stands at the top of Page.Content and scrolls up with the title; the content starts 16px under the title's baseline, and a list 10px under the field. With onClear it shows the filled clear circle of iOS while it holds text, in place of the browser's own clear button.

examples.name: Disabled
examples.code:
<Page surface="grouped">
<Toolbar>
  <Toolbar.Leading>
    <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" pill>Cancel</Button>
  </Toolbar.Leading>
  <Toolbar.Title>New order</Toolbar.Title>
  <Toolbar.Trailing>
    <NavigationButton action="confirm" disabled />
  </Toolbar.Trailing>
</Toolbar>
<Page.Content>...</Page.Content>
<Toolbar placement="bottom">
  <Toolbar.Leading>
    <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Filter" disabled><Filter /></Button>
  </Toolbar.Leading>
  <Toolbar.Content>
    <Button color="primary" pill disabled>Place order</Button>
  </Toolbar.Content>
  <Toolbar.Trailing>
    <Toolbar.Group aria-label="Order actions">
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Translate" disabled><Translate /></Button>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="More"><DotsHorizontal /></Button>
    </Toolbar.Group>
  </Toolbar.Trailing>
</Toolbar>
</Page>
examples.details: A disabled bar button keeps its glass capsule and draws its symbol or label in the tertiary label color, as the iOS 26 bar buttons do. Inside Toolbar.Group the capsule belongs to the group, so the enabled actions next to it keep their look. A prominent action, NavigationButton action="confirm" or a solid primary Button, drops its color for a gray capsule, with a white label in light and a dim one in dark. Cancel and More stay enabled.

examples.details: Tooltip provides an optional component, Tooltip.TriggerDecorator, to help create accessible tooltip triggers. However, any component can be used as a trigger.

examples.name: Conditionally enabled
examples.code:
<Tooltip
content={disabled ? "This action is disabled for reasons" : null}
>
<Button color="primary" size="lg" disabled={disabled}>
  Sample button
</Button>
</Tooltip>
examples.details: Sometimes a tooltip should only be disabled under certain conditions, such as when a component is disabled, providing more context as to why that is. Below is an example of how to do this by conditionally passing in null content.

examples.name: Compact tooltips
examples.code:
<Tooltip content="Copy to clipboard" compact>
<Button color="secondary" variant="ghost" size="md" aria-label="Copy to clipboard"><Copy /></Button>
</Tooltip>
examples.details: Compact tooltips are designed for short, 1-3 word tooltips with inverted styling. They feature minimal padding, a dark background with white text, and no box shadows. Use {'compact={true}'} for brief status messages.
